Amraphel
AM-ruh-fel
n. (the king of Shinar, one of the four eastern kings defeated by Abraham)
Hebrew Amraphel (H569), of disputed derivation, possibly Akkadian or Elamite in origin; king of Shinar, the region of ancient Babylonia.

Biblical Definition

Amraphel opens the roll call of the four eastern kings whose invasion of Canaan draws Abraham into his only recorded military campaign: “in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations” (Genesis 14:1). These four had held five Canaanite kings, including the king of Sodom, under tribute to Chedorlaomer for twelve years before a rebellion in the thirteenth year brought the eastern coalition west in force (Genesis 14:4), the same four named again as they mass against the rebels: “Chedorlaomer the king of Elam, and... Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five” (Genesis 14:9). Their victory swept up Lot, Abraham’s nephew, among the captives — the provocation that sent Abraham and his three hundred and eighteen trained servants in pursuit, resulting in a rescue so complete that “the king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that were with him, at the valley of Shaveh, which is the king’s dale” (Genesis 14:17) — the same meeting at which Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine to bless Abraham. Amraphel is thus part of the earliest recorded international military alliance in Scripture, and the earliest recorded instance of one of the patriarchs directly opposing an imperial coalition in battle.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Amraphel; he is the king of Shinar named first among the four eastern kings Abraham defeated in Genesis 14 to rescue his nephew Lot.

expand to see more

AMRAPHEL, n. A king of Shinar, one of four eastern kings defeated by Abraham in the rescue of Lot.

SHINAR, n. The ancient region of lower Mesopotamia, later the site of Babylon; the land of Amraphel and of the tower of Babel.

TRIBUTE, n. A stated sum or other valuable thing paid by one ruler or nation to another, in acknowledgment of submission.

ALLIANCE, n. A union or connection of interests between nations, kings, or parties, for mutual advantage or defense.

PATRIARCH, n. The father and ruler of a family; one of the progenitors of the Hebrew nation, such as Abraham.

Key Scripture

Genesis 14:1 — "And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations;"

Genesis 14:9 — "With Chedorlaomer the king of Elam, and with Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five."

Genesis 14:4 — "Twelve years they served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled."

Genesis 14:17 — "And the king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that were with him, at the valley of Shaveh, which is the king's dale."

Modern Corruption

A precisely named four-king eastern coalition, with a specific twelve-year tribute period and a datable political backdrop, is exactly the sort of concrete historical detail a late-invented patriarchal legend has no motive to manufacture.

expand to see more

Older critical scholarship dismissed Genesis 14 as a late, artificial insertion with no genuine historical background, in part because Amraphel's name was once thought impossible to place in the ancient Near East — a judgment increasingly qualified as cuneiform studies have clarified plausible Elamite and Mesopotamian political configurations of the general era, a pattern of the chapter's details becoming more, not less, historically credible as evidence accumulates rather than less.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Abraham's conduct after the victory: though entitled to the spoil his rescue had won, he refused it entirely from the king of Sodom, “lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich” (Genesis 14:23), while receiving Melchizedek's blessing and paying him tithes — a model of refusing entanglement with worldly power even in the moment of victory over it, and of honoring the LORD's true priest above every earthly king.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Amraphel (H569), of disputed derivation; Shin'ar (H8152), Shinar; melek (H4428), king; chalats (H2502), to draw out, rescue.

expand to see more

Hebrew Amraphel (H569) — of disputed derivation, possibly Akkadian or Elamite in origin.

Hebrew Shin'ar (H8152) — Shinar, the ancient region of lower Mesopotamia.

Hebrew melek (H4428) — king; the title borne by all four members of the eastern coalition.

Hebrew chalats (H2502) — to draw out, equip for war, rescue; Abraham's action in pursuing the captors.

Hebrew ma'aser (H4643) — tithe; what Abraham gave Melchizedek immediately after this victory.

Usage

"“In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar” — the opening of Genesis 14's account."

"“Four kings with five” — the scale of the ancient coalition warfare."

"“After his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that were with him” — Abraham's decisive victory."
